nameStory: The 'largeflower heartleaf' gets its name from its distinctive heart-shaped leaves and unusually large flowers compared to other wild gingers. The 'heartleaf' part is easy to see, but you'll have to look under those leaves to find the impressive urn-shaped blooms hiding at ground level. It's also called Shuttleworth's ginger after the botanist who first described it.
description: Largeflower heartleaf is a low-growing perennial wildflower that hugs the forest floor with glossy, heart-shaped leaves. This southeastern native rarely ventures into New England, making it an extremely rare find in our region. The plant stays close to the ground, with leaves typically reaching only 6-8 inches tall, and produces distinctive urn-shaped flowers that hide beneath the foliage. It's part of the wild ginger family, though it's not related to the spice we use in cooking.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Perfect heart-shaped leaves that are glossy and leathery to the touch, with prominent veining that creates a quilted texture on the surface

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large, urn-shaped flowers (bigger than other wild gingers) that hide directly at soil level beneath the leaves, often brownish-purple and requiring you to lift the foliage to see them

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Extremely low-growing plant that forms small colonies, with leaves emerging directly from underground rhizomes and staying close to the forest floor

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves feel thick and substantial when touched, remaining evergreen through winter and often showing silvery mottling patterns on the surface

habitat: In New England, this would be found in rich, moist deciduous forests with deep, well-draining soil, typically on protected slopes or in ravines. Given its southeastern origin, any New England occurrence would likely be in the warmer microclimates of southern areas, possibly in oak-hickory or mixed hardwood forests. The extreme rarity suggests it may only persist in very specific, sheltered locations with conditions similar to its native Appalachian habitat.

seasonality.spring: Flowers emerge in early spring directly from the soil beneath the leaves, often before many other woodland plants begin growing. The heart-shaped leaves may show fresh new growth emerging from the rhizomes.
seasonality.summer: Leaves remain glossy and prominent throughout summer, providing the main identifying feature since flowers will have finished blooming by mid-summer.
seasonality.fall: Evergreen leaves persist and may develop more pronounced silvery patterns or mottling, remaining visible as deciduous trees drop their canopy overhead.
seasonality.winter: The thick, leathery leaves often remain green through winter, making this one of the few herbaceous plants you can identify even in the coldest months.

funFact: The flowers of this plant are designed to trap flies and beetles temporarily - insects crawl into the urn-shaped bloom to reach nectar, but backward-pointing hairs prevent them from leaving until they're thoroughly coated with pollen, essentially turning the flower into a temporary insect prison!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with Canadian wild ginger, but largeflower heartleaf has much larger, showier flowers and leaves that tend to be more leathery and persistent through winter. Remember: if the leaves look extra glossy and thick, and the flowers seem unusually large for a wild ginger, you might have found this rare southeastern visitor.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'ginger,' this plant is completely unrelated to culinary ginger and shouldn't be eaten. The 'wild ginger' name comes from the slightly spicy scent of the crushed roots, which early settlers thought resembled true ginger. With only 2 recorded observations in New England, finding this plant would be an exceptional botanical discovery.
compareHints: Compared to its relative Canadian wild ginger, largeflower heartleaf has noticeably larger flowers (hence the name), more leathery evergreen leaves, and a more southern distribution. While Canadian wild ginger is fairly common in New England's rich woods, largeflower heartleaf is extremely rare here. The leaves of largeflower heartleaf also tend to be more glossy and substantial-feeling when touched, and they persist through winter unlike the more delicate foliage of Canadian wild ginger.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Canadian wild ginger is the only Asarum species commonly found in New England's forests.
Asarabacca differs from its North American cousin, wild ginger (Asarum canadense), by having evergreen leaves that are smaller and much more glossy.
Little Brown Jugs differs from Canadian wild ginger by having more arrow-shaped (rather than kidney-shaped) leaves and flowers that are more distinctly jug-shaped rather than bell-shaped.
